## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 6 notes, [*Data Visualisation Principles*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week06.html).

- Be able to map variables from data frames to aesthetics in `ggplot2`.
- Use common geometries (points, lines, bars, histograms and box plots).
- Use scales and coordinates, for example to zoom in on part of a plot or use a log scale.
- Summarise data before plotting to reveal patterns, such as trends hidden by seasonal variation.
- Recognise and avoid misleading plots.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions on the same data in `lab_06_practice.qmd`, including themes, facets, colourblind-safe palettes and violin plots.

### Task 1: Temperature Trends

The file `data/MET Office Weather Data.csv` contains monthly weather observations from 36 stations in the UK between 1853 and 2020.
The fields included are:

- **year**: Year in which the measurements were taken
- **month**: Month in which the measurements were taken
- **tmax**: Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)
- **tmin**: Mean daily minimum temperature (°C)
- **af**: Days of air frost recorded that month (days)
- **rain**: Total rainfall (mm)
- **sun**: Total sunshine duration (hours)
- **station**: Station location where measurement was recorded

The year and month are stored as integers. The first cell below reads the data and adds a new column called `date` using the `lubridate` `make_date` function.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
met <- read_csv("data/MET Office Weather Data.csv")
met <- met |>
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, 1))
head(met)
```

- [x] Produce a line plot showing how the maximum temperature in July recorded in the station in Southampton has changed over time. Add nice labels to your plot.
- [x] There appears to be a break in the plotted line. Work out where it is by using `coord_cartesian` to zoom in on the $x$ axis, and then check the dataset to identify the root cause. (Hint: look at the `xlim` argument of `coord_cartesian`. The $x$ axis shows dates, so the limits need to be dates too.)

::: {.solution}
Line Plot showing how max temp has changed in Southampton over time.
```{r}
max_temp_soton <- met |> filter(station == "southampton") |> filter(month == 7)|> ggplot(aes(x = year, y = tmax)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs( title = "Maximum temperature recoded in July in Southampton over time",
        x = "year",
        y = "mean maximum daily temperature")
max_temp_soton
```
we zoom in to see the break in better detail
```{r}
met |> filter(station == "southampton") |> filter(month == 7)|> ggplot(aes(x = year, y = tmax)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs( title = "Maximum temperature recoded in July in Southampton over time",
        x = "year",
        y = "mean maximum daily temperature") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1925, 1950)) 

#We zoom in even further
met |> filter(station == "southampton") |> filter(month == 7)|> ggplot(aes(x = year, y = tmax)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs( title = "Maximum temperature recoded in July in Southampton over time",
        x = "year",
        y = "mean maximum daily temperature") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1939, 1944))

```

Checking data set:
```{r}
met|> filter(station == "southampton") |> filter( year == 1941) 

```
We can see has NA values. (missing values)
:::

Next we look at every month of the year, not just July, at four stations.

- [x] Produce a scatter plot of the maximum temperature `tmax` against `date` for every month in Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley. Colour the points by station.
- [x] Look up the function `geom_smooth`. Use the function to overlay a smooth trend line on the points. Make sure the line is visible by adjusting the `alpha` property on `geom_point`.
- [x] What does the line tell you about the trend of historical maximum temperatures? It is going slightly upwards

::: {.solution}
```{r}
#| message: FALSE
max_temp1 <- met |> filter(station %in% c("southampton", "oxford", "sheffield", "paisley")) |> filter(is.na(tmax) == FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = station), alpha = 0.2) +
  labs( title = "Maximum temperature recoded in four cities over time",
        x = "date",
        y = "mean maximum daily temperature",
        colour = "Station") +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour= station), method = "lm", se = FALSE)
max_temp1
```
:::

The plot above mixes together every month of the year, so the seasonal cycle hides the long-term trend.
Averaging over each year removes the seasonal cycle, since every (complete) year contains one of each month.

- [ ] For each of Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley, compute the mean `tmax` in each year. Plot these annual means against `year` as a line plot, coloured by station, and add a smooth trend line. Is the trend easier to see now?
- [ ] Some of the annual means look suspicious. Which years have the lowest and highest annual means? How many months of data is each annual mean based on? (Hint: how would you count the *non-missing* values of a column inside `summarise`?)
- [ ] Redraw the plot using only years with a complete set of 12 months. Roughly how much have annual mean maximum temperatures risen at these stations?

::: {.solution}

### Task 2: Rainfall

- [x] Produce a bar chart showing how many monthly records there are for each station, using `geom_bar()`. Then produce the same chart using `count()` and `geom_col()`. (Hint: to make the station names readable, add `theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))` to your plot.)

::: {.solution}
```{r}
n_records_pl1 <- met |> ggplot(aes(x = station)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Number of monthly records per station", x = "Station", y = "Count") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
n_records1


n_records_pl2 <- met |>  group_by(station) |> summarise(n_records = n()) |>ggplot(aes(x = station, y= n_records)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Number of monthly records per station", x = "Station", y = "Count") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
n_records_pl2
```
OMG its the same exact graph

:::

- [x] Produce a bar chart showing the average rainfall (across all months and years) for the 5 stations with the highest average rainfall.
- [x] Now make a *deliberately misleading* version of this plot, which suggests that Cwmystwyth gets several times as much rain as Stornoway. Which of the principles in the Week 6 notes does your plot break? How could a reader spot the trick?

::: {.solution}
Find top 5 
```{r}
met |>  group_by(station) |> summarise(average_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE)) |> arrange(desc(average_rainfall)) |> head(5)
```
Bar chart of average rainfall

```{r}
rain_plot_1 <- met |>  group_by(station) |> summarise(average_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE)) |> arrange(desc(average_rainfall)) |> head(5) |> ggplot(aes(x = station, y = average_rainfall)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Average Rainfall for the wettest stations", x = "Station", y = "Average Rainfall")
rain_plot_1

rain_plot_2 <- met |>  group_by(station) |> summarise(average_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE)) |> arrange(desc(average_rainfall)) |> head(5) |> ggplot(aes(x = station, y = average_rainfall)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Average Rainfall for the wettest stations", x = "Station", y = "Average Rainfall") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 160))
rain_plot_2
```
The second plot breaks the principal of starting the bar charts at zero on the numerical axis.
:::

Bar charts of averages hide how much the rainfall varies from month to month, so next we look at its *distribution*.

- [x] Look up how to produce a box plot with `ggplot`, and produce a box plot of rainfall at each station. Are there any outliers at the low end? Why not?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
rain_plot_3 <- met |> group_by(station) |> ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Box plot of rainfall", x = "Station", y = "Rainfall") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
rain_plot_3
```
so many outliers but none at low end because standard deviation or length of IQR is too big to get outliers at low end. 
:::

- [ ] Plot a histogram of monthly rainfall across all stations. Experiment with the `bins` argument. How would you describe the shape of the distribution?
- [ ] Redraw the histogram with a logarithmic $x$ axis (see the Week 6 notes). What happens to the shape? Read the warning messages carefully, and compare the number of rows removed with the previous histogram. Which months have been dropped, and why?

::: {.solution}
